note: Platform enforcement events: the dates on which a platform stops accepting something, as opposed to the date a release line stops being maintained. endoflife.date models release lines well and these dates badly, because they belong to a vendor's policy rather than to the software. Each entry names the primary source it was read from and the date that source was last checked. Anything a live feed can answer is not duplicated here.

rules.headline: GitHub Actions runners remove Node 20
rules.detail: An action whose action.yml declares runs.using: node20 will not start once Node 20 is removed from the runner images. Node 24 became the default on 2026-06-16, and the ACTIONS_ALLOW_USE_UNSECURE_NODE_VERSION escape hatch stops working on the same day.
rules.fix: Upgrade to a release of the action that declares runs.using: node24.

rules.headline: Vercel disables Node 20 for builds and functions
rules.detail: New deployments of a project set to Node 20 fail from this date. Deployments already live keep serving, and containers are unaffected.
rules.fix: Raise the Node version in engines.node or .nvmrc and in the Vercel project settings.

rules.headline: Dependabot stopped supporting Python 3.9
rules.detail: Dependabot no longer opens dependency update pull requests for projects pinned to Python 3.9, so the repository silently stops receiving updates.
rules.fix: Raise the pinned Python version so dependency updates keep arriving.

rules.headline: Node 20 was removed from the runner toolcache
rules.detail: Node.js 20 was removed from the toolcache on all runner images between 2026-05-19 and 2026-05-26, and the default moved to Node 22 where Node 20 had been the default. A workflow asking for Node 20 now pays a download on every run instead of using the preinstalled copy.
rules.fix: Ask setup-node for a version that is still in the toolcache.

aws_lambda_phases.note: Lambda retires a runtime in three steps. Deprecation stops the patches. Block-create stops new functions. Block-update stops changing the ones you have, and that is the date that strands a service. endoflife.date publishes the deprecation and block-update dates for this product but not block-create, which is the earlier of the two enforcement events. AWS has repeatedly moved these dates later in response to customer feedback, so a stale copy is worse than none: this table records when it was last read from the AWS documentation.
aws_lambda_phases.supported_note: Runtime identifiers Lambda still accepts, read from the supported-runtimes table on the date above. A migration target is only offered if it appears here, so the tool never proposes a runtime AWS would reject.
